en: I took your Akshumkar,
Hurling empty slanderous words
And assailing me from this side!
When I wandered, my dear,
Did I traverse all the roads of the world?
Did I go demanding of your openhearted prince,
'Take me for yourself,'
And force myself upon him?
Did I take the falcon from your hand,
Saying, 'Give me its strength for six months'?
You stand saying, 'Give me my falcon';
How did I become subject to your claim?
You are young, my dear,
Yet you lay claim to your falcon.
As though you had taken a wife,
As though you were filled with joy,
You keep calling me 'sister-in-law.'
Whom do you think you are mocking?
You come right up to me
And begin addressing me as 'sister-in-law';
If I let you return to your own affairs,
You will still remain demanding the falcon.
What sort of outrageous boy are you?
As though you had taken a wife,
As though you had placed a bridal scarf upon my head,
You persist in calling me sister-in-law.
Do not lose your sense of propriety;
Set your words in order!
My husband is Chynkojo,
Tough as hardened red iron;
The husband who will take me is brave Toltoi,
Whose vastness equals half a mountain;
My nominal husband is Kadyrbai.
He is no enemy who merely stands and watches;
He rains arrows from the flank.
The husband I rely upon is like a mountain ridge,
And his courage is like blue steel.
Give my greetings and blessing
To your openhearted prince;
Do not let it be said that, coming for nothing,
He was killed by Toltoi."
When Külchoro had said this—
Surpassingly eloquent and also a lion,
The quick-witted boy Kulchoro—replied:
"The man upon whom you have set your hopes,
Whom you have found as your firm support,
Is he your famous husband Kojo?
I shall break down your fortress walls;
I shall smash to pieces
Your hulking fool of a husband, Toltoi!
You have found the Kara-Kyr ridge,
Over which even a goose will not circle, as your support;
You have found Tolok and Tolobai,
Kalcha and Kadyrbai,
The finest of the Jediger,
To be your husbands!
The men upon whom you have set your hopes—
If my precious head does not die,
I shall crush to flour
The husband destined to take you!
My uncle's Akshumkar
Does not gather its wings and swoop,
Nor send the geese flying from the lake;
It does not gather its tail and swoop,
Nor send the swans flying from the lake.
Upon Akshumkar's feet
Are finely fitted by Kanykei
Golden jesses with knobs.
May your road be fortunate, sister-in-law;
If you have lost the falcon,
Seventy maidens like you
Have a claim against you!
Its hood is exceedingly fine;
It has golden, knobbed jesses.
If you have lost the falcon,
Among maidens like you,
Ninety-one have a claim against you!
Let us announce the reward
For the falcon that disappeared;
If you make us wander, we shall turn back.
If you make us wander, sister-in-law,
The blame will fall upon your father, Khan Akun!"
When Aichurok heard this,
She sat looking sidelong
At Choro, the son of Almambet,
Taking in his full bearing.
She stood watching, deeply moved;
What could your dear sister-in-law do
But plead with Kulchoro:
"This Kulchoro standing here
Has every fortune in balance.
Except for his being a child,
His uncle Semetey
Must be an even greater lion than he.
There are boys of twelve
Who cannot manage to go out through the door,
Cannot cover their hems when they urinate,
And feel no shame before their mothers;
Far from speaking at length, those boys
Cannot utter two or three words.
For a boy such as this,
Let my dark life be a sacrifice!"
Having said this, Aichurok
Abandoned her taunting words
And began to speak plainly:
"My dear son,
What you said is also true.
Yesterday, stripping the weariness from my horse,
I flew and wandered
Throughout the whole wide world.
To distant Beijing and Kakan-Chyn,
I flew all the way;
Finding no upright hero to my liking,
I turned and came back.
Then, along the banks of Talas,
I found and chose my own husband.
Putting aside my wounded pride, poor wretch that I was,
I entered and moved among your village.
I placed my wishing necklace around my neck;
Saying, "Let him stay with you for six days,"
I pleaded with his wife.
Though I pleaded, the woman would not consent
And would not listen to my words.
Still aggrieved, poor wretch that I was,
I went to the edge of Ala-Kol
In the form of a white swan.
Thinking, "If my dear one is a man,
He will come in search of me,"
I remained beside Ala-Kol
In the form of a white swan,
And carried off
Your noble one's Akshumkar."
Having said this, Aichurok,
Her white throat gleaming,
Her moonlike face shining,
Took your sovereign's Buurul
To a plane tree stirred by the breeze
And tethered him securely there.
Without looking up or down,
Without thinking she might die,
Without looking all around,
Without valuing her life by so much as a hair,
When the laughing game began,

en: The boisterous young lord,
The champion upon whom the day had fallen,
Now lost all memory of himself.
The splendid one who had never seen a maiden
Saw the maiden and grew excited;
Calm and ringing with vigor,
Without valuing it as much as his boot-tip
That his mighty lord remained outside,
The overwhelmed Kulchoro,
Among thirty brides and thirty maidens,
With Aichurok in their midst,
Played on without concern.
The maidens' talk became a marvel;
As he sat playing in delight,
His lord passed out of his thoughts.
Let us leave the boy
With the maiden who delighted him,
And turn our story to the thoroughbred lord Semetey,
Who had given away Buurul and remained on foot.
Let us begin the news of him.
Upon the ridge of Agynek,
For that swaggering unfortunate man,
The sun before him darkened in the sky;
Sixty anxious thoughts
Came at once upon Semetey:
"Kulchoro, who was my shelter,
Has not yet passed twelve,
Has not come anywhere near fifteen;
The milk of Kanykei's breast
Has not yet left his palate.
He was a child whose understanding had not ripened,
Still awkward and unformed in himself.
Did he come to a high mountain pass
And fall to his death?
Did he come to a river with a fierce current
And drown in its waters?
Did he fall into a net
Bound round with iron rope?
Have enemies surrounded him on every side,
Has he fallen into their hands?
The decree laid down by God—
Has he met it?
He was a stouthearted boy;
Did he strike into a massed army
And fall dead?" he wondered.
His fire-like eyes blazed fiercely;
His true bloodlust seized him.
He threw the blue armor-coat around himself
And pleaded with the Almighty.
To train the spyglass upon the boy,
To learn news from the maidens,
He strained like a blue tiger
And made ready with the spyglass.
From an unexpected place no horse could cross,
From behind a low, forked rise,
He concealed his dark body
And cautiously raised his head;
He hid his whole frame
And brought his head into line.
He took the great spyglass inherited from Manas,
Turned its wheel,
And set it squarely to his eye;
He turned its screw
And focused it upon his eye.
When he turned the wheel,
That wondrous spyglass
Divided its lens into six,
And a road six days distant
Appeared clearly, without distortion.
Its lens was made of precious stone;
When he turned it to its full extent,
It divided into seven parts,
And a road seven days distant
Appeared as close as seven rope-lengths.
The great and precious spyglass
Was wound with gold inside;
Master caster Bolokbai
Had repaired every damaged place.
The lion grew furious,
Turned its wheel,
And set it squarely to his eye.
Beside the flowing river,
Across the plain of Great Opol,
The lion, the son of Manas,
Looked through the spyglass.
Without being consumed by grief or worry,
Without saying, "My uncle stands
Stranded behind me,"
Thirty brides and thirty maidens,

en: The immoderate Churok, and the boy—
All of them, struck with amazement,
Had gathered around him;
Look at their fawning attention:
They had encircled him.
Seeing this, Semetey thought:
"When he reaches his full maturity,
He will surely conquer a mighty realm;
When he grows into a true man,
When he equals the sons of heroes,
He will indeed show me
Marvels beyond imagining!
If this boy remains alive,
If he carries on like this, God will strike him;
He will unleash chaos.
The accursed wretch has gone wild
And will take my wife away;
Thus he will bring me to ruin.
That brazen wretch
Will carry off my wife.
He will put an end to my laughter;
That wretch will scatter
All the possessions I own!
